Propranolol is a beta blocker, a medicine used for heart problems, to help with some of the symptoms of anxiety and to prevent migraines.
For heart conditions, the NHS lists high blood pressure, irregular heartbeats such as atrial fibrillation and preventing chest pain from angina.
It is also used to lower the risk of future heart disease, heart attacks and strokes.
Propranolol can ease symptoms of an overactive thyroid, where it is usually used together with medicines that treat the thyroid.
In children, specialist hospital services describe propranolol liquid being used for infantile haemangiomas, which are vascular birthmarks.
note: GOSH and Newcastle pages per search summary.

sentence: Some of these specialist uses are described as off-label, meaning outside the manufacturer's licence, so guidance may differ.
In the UK it is available on prescription only, as tablets, slow-release capsules or a liquid.
Propranolol slows the heart rate so that the heart can pump blood more easily.
For anxiety, it blocks the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline, which drive physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating and shaking.
This means it treats the physical symptoms of anxiety rather than the worry itself.
The NHS says it usually starts to work within a few hours.
For heart conditions or high blood pressure the full effect can take 2 to 3 weeks.
For migraine prevention it can take several weeks to make a real difference, so the benefit is not immediate.

sentence: The NHS says most people have no side effects or only minor ones, and the common ones are usually mild and short-lived.
The most common are feeling dizzy or tired, cold hands or feet, difficulty sleeping and nightmares.
Some people get headaches, and less common effects include diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.

sentence: Dizziness is most likely when first starting or after a bigger dose, and the NHS says that anyone who feels dizzy should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery.
Rarer, more serious signs include easy bruising, breathlessness, swollen ankles and an irregular heartbeat.
Chest pain that does not settle needs a 999 call.
A serious allergic reaction, with swelling of the face or throat and difficulty breathing, is also an emergency that needs 999.
Other warning signs are usually raised with a GP or NHS 111 on the same day.

sentence: The NHS lists several situations where propranolol may not be suitable, including a past allergic reaction to it or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, and lung disease or asthma.
UK patient leaflets say that people who have ever had asthma or wheezing should not take propranolol tablets.
Diabetes is something to mention to the doctor before starting, because propranolol may make it harder to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar.
Leaflets add that it can change the usual response to low blood sugar and may cause low blood sugar even in people without diabetes.
On pregnancy, the NHS says propranolol can be taken but may sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra growth scans are usually offered from 32 weeks.
The NHS says breastfeeding is acceptable if the baby is healthy, because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk.
Some other NHS headache guidance does not recommend it in pregnancy, when planning a pregnancy or during breastfeeding, so a clinician weighs this up for each person.
The NHS says that other blood pressure medicines can sometimes lower blood pressure too much, causing dizziness or fainting.
Cold remedies, including pharmacy-bought ones, and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and naproxen are also listed, and NSAIDs may raise blood pressure.
A hospital leaflet lists medicines that slow the heart, such as digoxin, amiodarone, verapamil and diltiazem.
Alcohol can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect and cause dizziness or light-headedness.
The NHS describes stopping suddenly after long-term use as able to cause extra effects such as an irregular heartbeat, sweating and shaking.
This is why the prescriber normally lowers the dose gradually, and why any change is decided with them.
The NHS says blood pressure is checked regularly for people taking propranolol long term for migraines or anxiety.
For anxiety, the NHS says there do not seem to be lasting harmful effects from taking it for several months or years, and that it is best taken only for as long as needed.

Local NHS guidance is more cautious, so whether it suits a person is for their clinician to decide.
The NHS says propranolol will not stop contraception working.
However, the combined pill and contraceptive patch are not usually recommended with propranolol or other blood pressure medicines.
Vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea can also make the pill less effective.
